0.title: Last Words: The Final Letter of the Apostle Paul
0.overview:
There is a letter that reads like a last will and testament, a soldier’s final dispatch from the front, and a father’s farewell to his son — all at once. Paul writes 2 Timothy from a Roman dungeon, probably the Mamertine Prison below the Capitoline Hill, where prisoners awaited execution. He has already stood before Nero’s tribunal; he expects to stand there again, and this time he does not expect to survive. He has been abandoned by most of his colleagues. Demas has gone back to the world. The churches of Asia have turned away. The winter is coming and he has no cloak. Only Luke is with him.

And yet the letter is not a cry of despair but an act of faith. Paul is not finished. He is fighting, praying, thinking, teaching to the last. He writes to Timothy — the son of his heart, the young man he circumcised and took on mission, who is now in Ephesus struggling with false teachers and the creeping temptation to soft-pedal the gospel for the sake of peace — and he writes with the urgency of a man who knows the window is closing. Guard the deposit. Don’t be ashamed. Endure suffering. Preach the word. These are not polite suggestions; they are dying instructions.

The letter is the most personal in the Pauline corpus. More than anywhere else we see Paul the man: Paul who longs for Timothy’s tears, who is comforted by Onesiphorus’s courage, who feels the sting of Alexander’s opposition, who in his final lines sends greetings from people whose names he has not forgotten. The great apostle is a human being who is cold, lonely, and facing death — and whose faith in the Jesus who appears in this letter (“remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead”) is, in the end, the only thing that has not shaken.

The letter is addressed to the minister, but it speaks to every Christian who must hold something precious in a world that does not want it. The deposit Paul entrusts to Timothy — the gospel of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen — is the same deposit entrusted to every generation of the church. Guard it. Pass it on. It is worth dying for. Paul’s life proves the claim.

1.title: Guard the Deposit: Courage, the Gospel, and Faithful Examples
1.overview:
Chapter 1 opens with Paul’s most affectionate letter opening: he thinks of Timothy constantly, longs to see him, remembers his tears, and is confident of his genuine faith — a faith that lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. The warmth is not merely emotional; it is the foundation from which Paul presses his most urgent charge: stir up the gift of God in you, for God has not given us a spirit of fear but of power and love and self-control.

The theological engine of the chapter is the great gospel passage of vv. 8–12, where Paul — who is about to urge Timothy to suffer for the gospel — articulates what that gospel is: God’s sovereign purpose formed before time began, brought to light in the appearing of Jesus Christ who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. The foundation of courage is not personal confidence but the character of the One whose gospel we carry.

The chapter ends with two contrasting examples: the entire province of Asia, which has turned away from Paul, and Onesiphorus, who searched for the imprisoned apostle in Rome and was not ashamed of his chains. Timothy is being invited to choose between these two responses to the gospel and its herald.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul writes as an apostle by God's will, “according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus” (v.1) — to Timothy, his beloved child: grace, mercy and peace (v.2).

Both details matter. Paul is in Rome, in prison, and this time does not expect to come out; chapter 4 will say the time of his departure has come. These are the last written words we have from him — and he opens by naming his commission in terms of life. And where the first letter called Timothy “my true child in the faith”, set against the counterfeits then circulating, here he is “my beloved child.” The polemical edge is gone.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Personal Letter, Not a Church Order

There is no thanksgiving for a congregation here because no congregation is in view. 1 Timothy was a manual for a man running a difficult church; this is an old man writing to a younger one while there is still time. The difference shapes everything that follows — the tears remembered in verse 4, the grandmother named in verse 5, the request in chapter 4 to bring a cloak and some parchments.

'Mercy' appears in the greeting again, as in the first letter and nowhere in Paul's letters to churches. It is needed more here. Timothy is about to be asked to come to Rome, to a man in chains whom most people have abandoned, and to take up a deposit that has cost its previous holder everything.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: To be “his prisoner” (v.8) rather than Rome's is Paul's settled way of describing custody (Eph 3:1; Philem 1). The chain is real and the ownership is not.

Now: Notice that a man facing execution begins his final letter with “the promise of the life.” That is not bravado; it is the letter's whole argument stated in its first sentence, and everything else — do not be ashamed, share in suffering, guard the deposit — rests on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus, To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a word of this letter is read, know where it comes from. Paul is in Rome, in prison, and this time he does not expect to come out. He will say so plainly in chapter 4: the time of his departure has come. These are the last written words we have from him.

And the first thing he says about himself is that he is an apostle “according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus.” A man facing execution opens his final letter by naming his commission in terms of life. That is not bravado; it is the whole argument of the letter stated in the first sentence.

“By the will of God” — the same ground as always. Whatever a Roman court decides about him, his appointment did not come from anywhere a court can reach.

Then the address, and it has softened since the first letter. There Timothy was “my true child in the faith” — genuine, as against the counterfeits then circulating in Ephesus. Here he is “my beloved child.” The polemical edge is gone. Paul is not establishing Timothy's standing against rivals now; he is writing to somebody he loves.

“Grace, mercy, and peace” — mercy again, as in the first letter and nowhere in the letters to churches. And it is needed more here than there. Timothy is about to be asked to come to Rome, to a man in chains whom most people have abandoned, and to take up a deposit that has cost its previous holder everything.

It is a very short greeting, and there is no thanksgiving for a church because there is no church in view. This is a personal letter from an old man to a younger one, written while there was still time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–14 — Fan Into Flame, and Guard the Deposit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul thanks the God his ancestors served, with a clear conscience, remembering Timothy constantly night and day (v.3) — and remembering his tears, longs to see him and be filled with joy (v.4). He recalls Timothy's sincere faith, which lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (v.5).

So he reminds him to fan into flame the gift given through the laying on of Paul's hands (v.6), since God gave a spirit not of timidity but of power and love and self-control (v.7). Therefore he is not to be ashamed of the testimony, nor of Paul his prisoner, but to share in suffering by God's power (v.8) — the God who saved and called us, not because of our works but by his own purpose and grace, given in Christ before the ages began (v.9), now revealed through the appearing of our Saviour, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light (v.10).

For this Paul was appointed herald, apostle and teacher (v.11), and this is why he suffers — yet is not ashamed, for he knows whom he has believed and is convinced God can guard his deposit until that day (v.12). Timothy is to follow the pattern of sound words in faith and love (v.13), guarding the good deposit by the Holy Spirit who dwells in us (v.14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Deposits, Running Opposite Ways

Paratheke is the banking term from 1 Tim 6:20 — property left with a trustworthy man, to be returned exactly as received rather than developed or improved. It appears twice in this chapter, and the directions are opposite. In verse 12 Paul has entrusted something to God, and God is able to keep it. In verse 14 God has entrusted something to Timothy, and he must keep it — “by the Holy Spirit who dwells within us.” Both directions, same word, and the strength in both cases comes from the same place.

Verse 12's pronoun repays care: “I know whom I have believed”, not what. Paul's confidence at the end of his life does not rest on the soundness of his doctrine, though he fought for it in every letter he wrote. It rests on a person he is acquainted with. Doctrine matters enormously and it is not what a man leans on at the end; he leans on the one the doctrine is about.

And verses 9-10 are among the densest gospel statements in the New Testament. Grace was given “in Christ Jesus before the ages began” — not planned or intended but given, before there was a world in which we could exist to receive it, which removes any possibility that something we did since is the reason. Then it was “manifested” in history, and Christ “abolished death” — a verb meaning to render inoperative, in the past tense, written by a man on death row. Death still occurs; it no longer works.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verse 5 shows how the faith actually travelled. Acts tells us Timothy's mother was a believing Jewess and his father a Greek (Acts 16:1) — which almost certainly means the faith in that house came down the female line. Paul has spent two letters on overseers, deacons, ordination and public teaching; and the man he is entrusting everything to was formed by two women teaching a child at home, years before any of the machinery touched him. Nobody laid hands on Lois, and she is on no roll. He will make it explicit at 3:15: from childhood Timothy has known the sacred writings.

Now: The word in verse 7 is not the ordinary term for fear but deilia — cowardice, timidity, the shrinking that stops a man doing what he knows he should. Paul names it, which means it was there: Timothy was frightened, and the New Testament records it about one of its own leaders without embarrassment. The remedy is not “try to feel braver”. Paul tells a frightened man what he has been given — power because the task is beyond him, love because fear makes a man self-protective, and a sound mind because fear distorts judgement and a frightened man's estimate of his situation is almost never accurate. Note too that “fan into flame” implies embers, not ashes: the gift has not gone out, it needs air.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God whom I serve, as did my ancestors, with a clear conscience, as I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day. As I remember your tears, I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I thank God whom I serve, as did my ancestors, with a clear conscience.” Paul reaches back before his conversion. He does not treat his Jewish inheritance as a false start that Christ cancelled; the God he serves now is the God his forefathers served. The gospel was not a change of deity but the arrival of what that God had promised.

“With a clear conscience.” The letter to Ephesus made conscience a recurring test — the goal of the charge is love from a good conscience, and men who reject it make shipwreck (1 Tim 1:5, 19). Here Paul quietly claims the thing he required of others. It is the settled statement of a man at the end who has nothing outstanding.

“As I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day.” In a cell, with the hours empty, an old man prays for his friend at three in the morning. That is what the phrase means in practice.

Then verse 4, and it is one of the tenderest sentences Paul wrote: “As I remember your tears, I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.”

Somewhere there had been a parting, and Timothy had wept. Probably the last one, when Paul was taken. Paul remembers it, and the memory is precious rather than embarrassing to him. He does not tell Timothy that the tears were a weakness or that he should have borne it better.

“I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.” Not that Timothy may be comforted — that Paul may be. The man who has told other people to rejoice always, who is facing execution with composure, says openly that there is a joy he does not yet have and that a visit from this young man would supply it. Contentment in Paul never meant needing nobody.

verseByVerse.quote: I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I am reminded of your sincere faith” — anypokritos, un-play-acted, without a mask, the same word used of the faith the whole charge aims at in 1 Timothy 1:5. Whatever Timothy's timidity, Paul has no doubt his faith is the genuine article.

Then the two names, and this is one of the loveliest verses in the New Testament: “a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.”

Three generations, named. Acts tells us Timothy's mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek (Acts 16:1) — which almost certainly means the father was not a believer, and that the faith in that house came down the female line. A grandmother, then a mother, then a boy who would carry the apostolic deposit into the next generation.

Weigh what that means about how the faith actually travels. Paul has spent two letters on overseers, deacons, elders, ordination and public teaching. And the man he is entrusting everything to was formed by two women teaching a child at home, years before any of the machinery touched him. Nobody laid hands on Lois. She is not on any roll. She taught her daughter, who taught her son, and the result is the letter you are reading.

Paul will make it explicit in chapter 3: from childhood Timothy has known the sacred writings (3:15). Somebody sat with him and taught him the Scriptures before he could read them himself, and it was not an apostle.

“And now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.” The verb dwells is the word for taking up residence — faith is not visiting Timothy, it lives there. And “I am sure” is Paul's own judgement, offered to a man who evidently needed to hear it. Some people require someone else to tell them that what they have is real.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands, for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God.” The verb means to rekindle, to stir a fire back into blaze — and it implies embers rather than ashes. Paul does not think the gift has gone out. He thinks it needs air.

That is a gentle diagnosis of a real condition. Timothy is not accused of unbelief or failure. He is a man whose fire has burned low — which happens to people who have been under pressure for a long time in a difficult post, and the apostolic response is not rebuke but stirring.

“Which is in you through the laying on of my hands.” Note the difference from the first letter, where the gift came “when the council of elders laid their hands on you” (1 Tim 4:14). Both are true — Paul was among them — but here he presses the personal connection, because that is what this letter is doing. The old man who commissioned him is about to die, and he wants Timothy to remember whose hands were on his head.

Then verse 7, which is the reason the fire had dimmed: “God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.”

The word is not the ordinary term for fear but deilia — cowardice, timidity, the shrinking that stops a man doing what he knows he should. Paul names it, which means it was there. Timothy was frightened, and the New Testament records it about one of its own leaders without embarrassment.

Against it, three gifts, and each answers something. Power — because the task is beyond him, and it always was. Love — because fear makes a man self-protective, and love is the only thing that reliably gets him outside himself. And self-control, sophronismos, a sound and disciplined mind — because fear distorts judgement, and a frightened man's estimate of his situation is almost never accurate.

The three together are the answer to timidity, and none of them is “try to feel braver”. Paul tells a frightened man what he has been given, not what he ought to summon.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore do not be ashamed.” The word governs this chapter — it comes three times (here, v.12, v.16) and shame is the pressure Timothy is under.

Two things he might be ashamed of, and they are named separately. First, “the testimony about our Lord” — the message itself, which in the Roman world meant announcing that a crucified provincial was Lord. Crucifixion was not a symbol then; it was the death reserved for slaves and rebels, and to preach it was to invite the response Paul got at Athens.

Second, and more pointedly: “nor of me his prisoner.” There is the real difficulty. Paul is in custody awaiting execution, and association with him is dangerous and humiliating. Verse 15 will say that everyone in Asia has already turned away. Timothy is being asked to be publicly connected to a condemned man at the exact moment when everyone else has decided not to be.

Note how Paul describes himself: not Rome's prisoner but his — the Lord's. The chain is real and the custody is Roman, but the ownership is not. He said the same thing from an earlier imprisonment (Eph 3:1; Philem 1).

“But share in suffering for the gospel.” The verb is a compound — suffer together with. Paul is not asking Timothy to be brave in his own separate trouble but to come and take a share of this one. It is an invitation into something, not merely an exhortation to endure.

And the clause that makes it possible: “by the power of God.” Not by Timothy's resolve. Paul has just said God gave a spirit of power (v.7), and here is where it is spent. The courage being asked for is not a quality Timothy must find in himself; it is a supply he is told to draw on.

verseByVerse.quote: who saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began, and which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has asked Timothy to suffer by the power of God — and then, characteristically, cannot mention God without describing him. What follows is one of the densest statements of the gospel in the New Testament, and it has the compression of something already sung.

“Who saved us and called us to a holy calling.” Both verbs are past and both are God's. Then the negative and the positive, and Paul is emphatic about the order: “not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace.”

“Which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began.” Stop there, because it is one of the most staggering phrases Paul ever wrote. Grace was given to us before time started. Not planned, not intended — given, in Christ Jesus, before there was any world in which we could exist to receive it. Whatever else that means, it removes the possibility that anything we have done since is the reason.

Then verse 10 brings it into history: “and which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Saviour Christ Jesus.” The eternal purpose stayed hidden until a particular arrival. Epiphaneia is the shining-out word, used in that world of a god's or a king's public appearance.

“Who abolished death.” The verb means to render inoperative, to put out of action, to strip of power. And it is past tense — written by a man on death row. Paul does not say death has been made pleasant or that it will one day be dealt with. He says it has already been disarmed. It still occurs; it no longer works.

“And brought life and immortality to light through the gospel.” The image is of something switched on. Immortality was a hope people argued about — philosophers debated it, mystery cults sold it, tombstones denied it. Paul says it is no longer a matter of speculation, because it has been illuminated by an event.

And notice where this sits. Paul writes it to persuade a frightened young man to come and share his suffering. The argument is not “be brave”; it is “death has been abolished, so what exactly are they threatening you with?”

verseByVerse.quote: for which I was appointed a preacher and apostle and teacher, which is why I suffer as I do. But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For which I was appointed a preacher and apostle and teacher” — herald, sent one, instructor, the same three offices as 1 Timothy 2:7. “Which is why I suffer as I do.” The suffering is not an interruption of the appointment; it is the consequence of it.

“But I am not ashamed.” There is the word again, and now Paul applies it to himself. He has told Timothy not to be ashamed of a prisoner; here he says the prisoner is not ashamed either. He is not asking the young man to bear something he is privately embarrassed about.

Then the sentence that has held Christians steady for two thousand years: “for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.”

Read the pronoun carefully. Not what I have believed — whom. Paul's confidence at the end of his life does not rest on the soundness of his doctrine, though he has fought for it in every letter. It rests on a person he is acquainted with. Doctrine matters enormously and it is not what you lean on at the end; you lean on the one the doctrine is about.

“He is able to guard.” The deposit language again (1 Tim 6:20), and here it runs the other way. Paul had a deposit to guard, and he tells Timothy in two verses to guard his. But underneath both is this: Paul has made a deposit with God, and God is keeping it. The guarding Christians do is real and it is not the guarding that finally counts.

What is the deposit he has left with God? He does not specify, and the ambiguity is probably deliberate — his own life, his converts, the gospel, all of it. Everything a man cannot hold on to himself, lodged with someone who can.

“Until that day.” Not until the trial, or until the executioner, or until things improve. Paul's horizon runs past his own death without pausing at it.

verseByVerse.quote: Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me.” The word is hypotyposis — an outline, a sketch, a model to work from, the same word Paul used of himself as the pattern of Christ's patience (1 Tim 1:16). Timothy is not being told to reproduce Paul's sentences verbatim; he is given a shape to keep to.

“Sound words” — the medical word again, healthy, wholesome. And “that you have heard from me”, which is the chain this letter keeps tracing: entrusted to Paul, heard by Timothy, to be handed on to faithful men who will teach others (2:2).

“In the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.” The pattern is not held in a vacuum. Doctrine kept without faith and love becomes exactly what the Ephesian teachers had — correct-sounding material producing envy and friction.

Then verse 14: “Guard the good deposit entrusted to you.” Paratheke, the banking term from 1 Timothy 6:20 — property left with a trustworthy man, to be returned exactly as received. Not developed, not improved. Returned.

And the clause that makes the command bearable: “by the Holy Spirit who dwells within us.” Timothy is not being asked to defend the faith with his own resources, which is just as well, since he is timid and Paul is about to die and everyone in Asia has left. The guarding is done by someone who lives inside the guard.

Set the two deposits side by side and the chapter's architecture appears. In verse 12 Paul has entrusted something to God, and God is able to keep it. In verse 14 God has entrusted something to Timothy, and he must keep it — by God's own Spirit. Both directions, same word, and the strength in both cases comes from the same place.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All who are in Asia have turned away from Paul, Phygelus and Hermogenes among them (v.15). But may the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, who often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chains (v.16) — who on reaching Rome searched hard for him and found him (v.17); may the Lord grant him to find mercy on that day, and Timothy knows well all the service he rendered at Ephesus (v.18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Shame, and the Man Who Refused It

“Ashamed” governs this chapter, appearing three times — the pressure Timothy is under (v.8), the pressure Paul refuses (v.12), and here the pressure one man ignored (v.16). Note that Paul specifies the chains: it was the visible, humiliating, incriminating fact of the imprisonment that others could not stomach.

The turning away of verse 15 is probably not apostasy but personal desertion. Association with a man awaiting execution on a capital charge was genuinely dangerous, and people who had truly believed the gospel decided they could not afford to be connected with the prisoner — a more ordinary failure, and a more likely one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Asia is the province whose capital is Ephesus, where Paul spent three years — longer than anywhere else — teaching daily in the hall of Tyrannus until all the residents of the province had heard the word (Acts 19:10). His most fruitful work. And at the end they turned away. Phygelus and Hermogenes appear once in Scripture and it is here, for this; Paul evidently thought Timothy should know who they were, presumably because they were men he would otherwise have trusted.

Now: The detail that makes Onesiphorus unforgettable is in verse 17. Rome held perhaps a million people; a prisoner awaiting trial was listed nowhere convenient, and asking after a man on a capital charge meant drawing official attention to yourself. He went round the city making exactly the enquiries a sensible man would avoid, until he found him — and did it more than once. He preached no sermon we know of and held no office we are told about. Paul's prayer for a man who searched is that he would find mercy, and the echo is surely deliberate. That is this chapter's answer to shame, and it is available to anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.”

It is one of the saddest verses in the New Testament, and it should not be hurried past. Asia is the province whose capital is Ephesus — where Paul spent three years, longer than anywhere else, teaching daily in the hall of Tyrannus until all the residents of the province had heard the word (Acts 19:10). It was his most fruitful work.

And at the end, they turned away from him. “All” is doubtless a generalisation with exceptions — the next verse names one — but it is what it felt like from the cell.

The turning away is probably not apostasy. It reads as personal desertion: association with a man awaiting execution on a capital charge was dangerous, and people who had genuinely believed the gospel decided they could not afford to be connected with the prisoner. Which is a more ordinary failure, and a more likely one.

Two names are given, and we know nothing else about them. Phygelus and Hermogenes appear once in Scripture, and it is here, for this. That is a sobering way to be remembered — and Paul evidently thought Timothy should know who they were, presumably because they were men Timothy would otherwise have trusted.

What matters most is the effect of this on the letter's central request. Paul is asking Timothy not to be ashamed of him (v.8) and to come to him (4:9, 21) — and he tells him plainly, before he asks, that everybody else has already declined. He does not conceal how isolated he is or make the invitation look more attractive than it is. He puts the cost on the table and then asks anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains, but when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me— may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day!—and you well know all the service he rendered at Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against the desertion of verse 15, one man. “May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus.”

We know nothing about him except these three verses and a passing mention in chapter 4. He is one of the minor figures of Scripture who exists in a sentence and turns out to be unforgettable.

Three things are said about him, and they build. “He often refreshed me” — the verb means to cool, to give respite, the relief of shade or water. Not once but often. Whatever the practical content — food, news, conversation, money — a man in a Roman cell was regularly made more comfortable because Onesiphorus kept turning up.

“And was not ashamed of my chains.” There is the chapter's word for the third time, and here it is answered. Everyone in Asia had been ashamed; this man was not. Note that Paul specifies the chains rather than the man — it was the visible, humiliating, incriminating fact of the imprisonment that others could not stomach.

“But when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me.” This is the detail that makes the portrait. Rome was a city of perhaps a million people; a prisoner awaiting trial was not listed anywhere convenient, and asking after a man on a capital charge meant drawing official attention to yourself. Onesiphorus went round Rome making exactly the enquiries a sensible man would avoid, until he found him.

“May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day.” Paul's prayer for a man who searched is that he would find — and the echo is surely deliberate. He sought Paul out; may he be sought out and shown mercy.

The chapter that began with a frightened young man and a deserted apostle ends with a portrait of one ordinary Christian who simply turned up. He preached no sermons we know of and held no office we are told about. He looked for a prisoner until he found him, and did it more than once, and was not embarrassed to be seen there. That is the answer this letter gives to shame, and it is available to anybody.

But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.<sup>13</sup>Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.<sup>14</sup>By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you.<sup>15</sup>You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.<sup>16</sup>May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains,<sup>17</sup>but when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me—<sup>18</sup>may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day!—and you well know all the service he rendered at Ephesus.

2.title: Soldier, Athlete, Farmer: The Shape of Gospel Ministry
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is Paul’s most concentrated instruction on the nature of gospel ministry. Three images in rapid succession — soldier, athlete, farmer — define the minister’s posture: single-mindedly devoted, rule-governed, and patiently laboring for a harvest that is certain though not yet visible. The minister is not someone who has found an easier life; they have exchanged one set of hardships for another and found the exchange worthwhile.

The chapter’s centre is the trustworthy saying of vv. 11–13 — almost certainly an early hymn known to Timothy — which holds together the certainty of future glory and the seriousness of present faithfulness. The logic of endurance is not stoic grit but eschatological confidence: if we died with him we will live with him; if we endure we will reign with him.

The second half of the chapter shifts to the pastoral work of handling false teachers and navigating community conflict. The worker approved by God rightly handles the word of truth, avoids quarrelling, and corrects opponents with gentleness, recognising that God may yet grant them repentance. The minister’s posture toward error is not the prosecutor’s fury but the physician’s patience.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — A Good Soldier of Christ Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Timothy is to be strengthened by grace (v.1), and to entrust what he heard from Paul to faithful men who can teach others (v.2). He is to share in suffering as a good soldier (v.3), who does not get entangled in civilian affairs since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him (v.4); as an athlete, who is not crowned unless he competes by the rules (v.5); as the hard-working farmer, who should have the first share of the crops (v.6). Let him think it over, and the Lord will give understanding (v.7).

Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as in Paul's gospel (v.8) — for which he suffers, chained as a criminal; but the word of God is not bound (v.9). So he endures everything for the sake of the elect, that they may obtain salvation with eternal glory (v.10). The trustworthy saying follows: if we died with him we shall live with him (v.11); if we endure we shall reign, if we deny him he will deny us (v.12); if we are faithless he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself (v.13).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Broken Symmetry of Verse 13

The hymn's four lines do not all run the same way, and the fourth is why it is loved. The first three match our action with a corresponding response — died with him, live with him; endure, reign; deny, be denied. The fourth breaks the pattern: we are faithless, and he is faithful. The symmetry fails, and it fails in our favour.

The third and fourth lines are reconciled by a real distinction. To deny is to repudiate, to disown deliberately and finally. To be faithless is to fail, to let him down, to be the sort of Christian who keeps collapsing. Peter did both on the same night, and what separated him from Judas was not the size of the failure but what happened afterwards. And the ground of the fourth line is not our sincerity but God's nature — “he cannot deny himself.” His faithfulness is not a policy he might revise; abandoning someone he has taken would require him to stop being what he is.

Verse 2 is meanwhile among the most consequential sentences in the New Testament for the survival of the faith. Count the links: Paul heard it from Christ, Timothy from Paul, Timothy is to entrust it to faithful men, and they will teach others — four generations in one sentence, arranged from a death cell. The criterion is a single adjective: faithful. Not gifted, not clever. Reliable.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The three images each add something. The soldier — singleness of aim; 'civilian pursuits' are not sinful things but ordinary ones, and the point is that a man on active service has accepted a limit on how much of ordinary life he can carry, because he can be moved at any hour. The athlete — discipline, and the Greek games disqualified a man for what he did in training as well as in the contest. The farmer — time, which the other two lack: a soldier's engagement is settled in a day, a farmer works months and sees nothing. Timothy needed all three, and the third most.

Now: Note the balance of verse 7 — Paul hands over three pictures without explaining them, tells Timothy to think hard, and promises the Lord will give understanding. Both halves stand. The man who waits for insight without labouring will not get it; the man who labours as though it depends on his cleverness has misunderstood where it comes from. And verse 9's exclamation is worth remembering whenever the church looks contained: preachers can be silenced and Bibles confiscated, but the sentence written in that cell has travelled further than any of the men who put him there.

verseByVerse.quote: You then, my child, be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus, and what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You then, my child, be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus.” The verb is passive — be strengthened, let yourself be made strong. Paul does not tell a timid man to be strong; he tells him to be strengthened, and names the supply. Grace is not only what pardons; it is what powers.

Then verse 2, which is one of the most consequential sentences in the New Testament for the practical survival of the faith: “what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.”

Count the links. Paul heard it from Christ. Timothy heard it from Paul. Timothy is to entrust it to faithful men. Those men will teach others. Four generations in one sentence — and Paul is writing from a death cell, arranging for the deposit to outlive him by three hands.

The verb is the deposit word again, parathou, from the banking term of 1:14. The gospel is being lodged with somebody for safekeeping, and the criterion for choosing them is given in a single adjective: faithful. Not gifted, not clever, not impressive. Reliable. A man you can leave something with.

And the second criterion is capability rather than brilliance: “able to teach others also.” The point of the chain is that it keeps going. A man who can receive but not pass on is a terminus, however sound he is.

This is how the faith has actually reached anyone reading this. Not chiefly through institutions or movements but through a long series of individuals who received something and handed it to somebody else, most of them unrecorded. Paul's arrangement for the future of Christianity, made under sentence of death, was to tell one young man to find some reliable people.

verseByVerse.quote: Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.” The same compound verb as 1:8 — suffer together with — and the first of three images that follow in quick succession.

The soldier is chosen for a specific quality, and Paul names it: “No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him.”

The word for entangled means to be woven into, caught up in. And “civilian pursuits” is literally the affairs of life — not sinful things, but ordinary ones. Business, property, domestic arrangements. Paul is not saying a soldier must have no life; he is saying that a man on active service has accepted a restriction on how much of ordinary life he can carry, because he can be moved at any hour.

“His aim is to please the one who enlisted him.” That is the definition of the soldier's freedom and his constraint together. He has exactly one person to satisfy — which simplifies a great many decisions, and rules out a great many others.

Applied to Timothy, in a church full of people with opinions about him, this is a considerable relief. He is not required to satisfy the congregation, the older men who resent him, or the teachers he is opposing. One audience, one commanding officer.

And it should be read with care rather than as a charter for neglect. Paul has just spent a letter insisting that a man manage his own household well and provide for his relatives (1 Tim 3:4; 5:8). The soldier image is not permission to abandon ordinary duties; it is a warning against being so woven into comfort and property that you cannot be moved when the order comes.

verseByVerse.quote: An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops. Think over what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two more images, and each adds something the soldier did not carry.

“An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules.” The crown is the victor's wreath. And the condition is exact: lawfully, by the rules — which in the Greek games included the required months of training before the contest as well as the conduct of it. A man could win the race and be disqualified for what he did beforehand.

The point is that effort alone does not qualify anybody. There is a right way to do this work, and energy expended outside it earns nothing — which is a word to the hard-working minister who has quietly stopped caring how he gets results.

“It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops.” The adjective is the labouring word, kopionta, work to exhaustion. And the farmer brings what the other two lack: time. A soldier's engagement is decided in a day, an athlete's in an afternoon. A farmer works for months and sees nothing at all, and if he stops because nothing is visible there will be no harvest.

Between them the three images cover the whole of Christian service. The soldier — singleness of aim, and readiness to be moved. The athlete — discipline, and playing by the rules. The farmer — patience, and long labour before anything shows. Timothy needed all three, and the third one most.

Then verse 7, and it is a small masterpiece of teaching method: “Think over what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.”

Paul does not explain the three pictures. He hands them over and tells Timothy to work at them — and then promises that the understanding will be given. Both halves are there and neither cancels the other. Hard thinking is commanded; illumination is God's gift. The man who waits for insight without labouring will not get it, and the man who labours as though it depends on his own cleverness has misunderstood where it comes from.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel, for which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound!
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David.” Two clauses, and they are the whole gospel in shorthand: risen — so he is Lord and death is beaten; offspring of David — so he is genuinely human and the promises to Israel have been kept in him.

The participle is perfect: having been raised, and remaining so. Not an event in the past that occurred and finished, but a standing condition. There is a risen man.

And the command is simply to remember. Paul does not tell Timothy to work something out or achieve something. Under pressure the things you know perfectly well stop being present to you, and the remedy is recollection. It is what the Lord's Supper is for.

“As preached in my gospel” — not a rival version, but the message committed to him (1 Tim 1:11). “For which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal.” The word is kakourgos, a malefactor — the same term Luke uses of the two men crucified beside Jesus (Luke 23:32). Paul is classified with the worst.

Then the sentence that lifts the paragraph off the page: “But the word of God is not bound!”

The exclamation is in the Greek. Paul is chained; the word is not. Rome can hold the apostle and can do nothing whatever to the message. And the proof is in your hands — the sentence written in that cell has travelled further than any of the men who put him there.

It is a good thing to remember whenever the church looks contained. Preachers can be silenced, buildings closed, Bibles confiscated, ministries ended by illness. None of that touches the word itself, which has never yet been successfully imprisoned by anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect.” The word means to remain under a weight without buckling. And “everything” is not rhetoric from this man — he has the list elsewhere: floggings, stonings, shipwrecks, hunger, and now a Roman death cell.

But note the reason, because it is not the one we might expect. Not for the sake of Christ, though that is true and he says it elsewhere. Not for his own reward. “For the sake of the elect” — for people.

Sit with that. Paul's motive at the end of his life is a group of human beings, most of whom he has never met and some of whom are not yet born. His suffering is not merely borne; it is spent on somebody.

“The elect” raises the obvious question, and Paul answers it in the same breath by what he does. If God has chosen a people, why endure anything? Why not leave him to it? The answer is the purpose clause: “that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus.”

Election has never in Scripture been a reason for inaction; it is the reason the action is worth taking. Paul knows there are people God has chosen, so he knows his labour is not a gamble. He does not know who they are, so he preaches to everyone and endures anything to reach them. Certainty about the outcome produces energy, not idleness. It was the same logic that kept him in Corinth: I have many in this city who are my people (Acts 18:9-10).

“With eternal glory.” The last word of the verse sets the whole thing in proportion — everything endured, weighed against what it purchases, and the purchase is not temporary.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy, for: If we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful— for he cannot deny himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The saying is trustworthy” — the fourth of the five formulas, and what follows has the balance and rhythm of a hymn. Four conditional lines, and they do not all run the same way.

“If we have died with him, we will also live with him.” Past tense — this happened, at conversion, in union with Christ. The dying is behind; the living is certain.

“If we endure, we will also reign with him.” Present and continuing. The word is the one from verse 10, remaining under weight. And the promise attached is startlingly large: not merely survival but reigning.

Then the line turns dark. “If we deny him, he also will deny us.” It is the Lord's own word (Matt 10:33), and it is not softened here. Settled, final denial has a settled, final answer.

And then the fourth line, which is the reason this hymn is loved: “If we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself.”

Read carefully, because the pattern breaks. The first three lines match our action with a corresponding response. The fourth does not. We are faithless, and he is — faithful. The symmetry fails, and it fails in our favour.

How does this sit with the third line? The distinction is between denying and failing. To deny is to repudiate, to disown deliberately and finally. To be faithless is to fail, to let him down, to be the sort of Christian who keeps collapsing. Peter did both on the same night — he denied, and it was faithlessness — and the difference between him and Judas was not the size of the failure but what happened afterwards.

And the ground of the fourth line is not our sincerity but God's nature: “he cannot deny himself.” His faithfulness is not a policy he might revise. To abandon someone he has taken would require him to stop being what he is, and that is the one thing he cannot do. Written to a frightened man by a dying one, it is the most reassuring sentence in the letter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–26 — A Worker Approved by God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Timothy is to remind them and charge them before God not to quarrel about words, which does no good and ruins the hearers (v.14) — but to do his best to present himself approved to God, a worker unashamed, rightly handling the word of truth (v.15). He is to avoid irreverent babble, which leads to more ungodliness (v.16) and spreads like gangrene, as with Hymenaeus and Philetus (v.17), who say the resurrection has already happened and are upsetting some people's faith (v.18).

But God's firm foundation stands, sealed with two lines: the Lord knows those who are his, and let everyone who names his name depart from iniquity (v.19). In a great house there are vessels of gold and silver and also of wood and clay (v.20); whoever cleanses himself becomes a vessel for honourable use, holy, useful to the master, ready for every good work (v.21).

So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart (v.22). Have nothing to do with foolish controversies, which breed quarrels (v.23). The Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil (v.24), correcting opponents with gentleness — God may perhaps grant them repentance (v.25), so that they come to their senses and escape the devil's snare, having been captured to do his will (v.26).
verseByVerse.theology:
Cutting Straight

The phrase everything turns on in verse 15 is orthotomeo — literally to cut straight. It is used of cutting a straight road, and of a stonemason or leatherworker cutting material accurately so the pieces fit. Paul was a leatherworker, and anyone who has watched a cutter at a bench knows the force of it: the material is expensive, the cut is irreversible, and a line that wanders ruins the piece. A crooked cut cannot be uncut.

So what Paul commends is not eloquence or enthusiasm but accuracy — giving what is actually in the text rather than what the preacher would like to be there. And set against verse 14 it is the whole alternative: the word-fighters use Scripture as ammunition; the approved worker handles it like a man who will answer for every cut. Note also who the audience is — 'present yourself to God', not to the congregation or the critics.

The seal of verse 19 has two lines facing opposite ways, and both are needed. “The Lord knows those who are his” is quoted from Num 16:5, Moses' answer when Korah's rebellion made it unclear who genuinely belonged to God — exactly Timothy's situation. The register is not kept by us, and God's knowledge is unaffected by our confusion. Then “let everyone who names the name depart from iniquity” is our side: assurance rests on God's knowing, and the evidence of belonging is the departure. A foundation with only one of those lines on it will not hold a building up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Hymenaeus was handed over to Satan in the first letter, that he might learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim 1:20). He is still at it and has acquired a colleague — discipline had been applied and had not worked, which the New Testament records without pretending otherwise. Their error, that the resurrection has already happened, was almost certainly a spiritualising of it: attractive because it sounds advanced and requires nothing to be waited for. But if resurrection has already occurred, the Christians in the ground have missed it and everyone still suffering has nothing coming — the identical wreckage the Thessalonians suffered (2 Thess 2:2), landing on the grieving first.

Now: Verse 14 makes the sharpest observation in the chapter and it is easily missed. Word-fights damage the hearers, not the combatants, who are usually enjoying themselves. Somebody in the room is new in the faith or barely holding on, and what they learn is that Christianity is a thing people shout about. Note too what verse 21 does not say: faced with frauds in the house, Timothy is not told to audit everybody else but to cleanse himself — and the classification is not fixed, since a vessel can move category. And verse 25 explains why gentleness is not weakness: repentance is God's to grant. If the outcome depended on the teacher's argument, overwhelming force would be the sensible tactic. Paul's picture of his opponents is not that they are villains but that they are caught — taken alive, doing another's will while believing it is their own.

verseByVerse.quote: Remind them of these things, and charge them before God not to quarrel about words, which does no good, but only ruins the hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Remind them of these things, and charge them before God not to quarrel about words.”

The verb is logomachein — literally to word-fight, and it is the same disease diagnosed at Ephesus in the first letter (1 Tim 6:4). Paul has been dealing with it for years and it has not gone away.

Note the solemnity: “charge them before God.” This is the oath language of 1 Timothy 5:21 and 2 Timothy 4:1. Paul does not treat quarrelling about words as a minor irritation to be managed. He puts the congregation under oath about it.

Then the verdict, in two parts. It “does no good” — literally it is useful for nothing, profitable in no respect. Whatever else may be said for a theological argument conducted this way, nobody is better for it.

“But only ruins the hearers.” The word is katastrophe — overturning, subversion, the collapse of a structure. And notice who suffers it. Not the combatants, who are usually enjoying themselves, but the hearers — the people in the room who did not want the fight and have to watch it.

That is the sharpest observation in the verse and it is easily missed. Word-fights always have an audience, and the audience takes the damage. Somebody sitting there is new in the faith, or barely holding on, and what they learn is that Christianity is a thing people shout about. The participants go home invigorated. The hearers are what is left over, and something in them has come down.

Set against it is verse 15's alternative, and the contrast is the point: not quarrelling about the word, but rightly handling it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved.” The verb means to be diligent, to make every effort — and the audience is named at once. Not the congregation, not the critics in Ephesus. To God.

“One approved” is dokimos, the assayer's word for metal that has been tested and passed. It is the standing image of this correspondence (1 Tim 3:10) and it implies the test has already happened.

“A worker who has no need to be ashamed.” There is the chapter-one word again, and here it is turned inside out. Timothy was told not to be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul; now he is told to work in such a way that his own labour gives him nothing to be ashamed of. The picture is a craftsman looking at what he has made and not needing to apologise for it.

Then the phrase everything turns on: “rightly handling the word of truth.” The Greek is orthotomeo — literally to cut straight. It is used of cutting a straight road, and of a stonemason or a leatherworker cutting material accurately so the pieces fit.

Paul was a leatherworker. Anyone who has watched a cutter at a bench knows what the image means: the material is expensive, the cut is irreversible, and a line that wanders wastes the hide and ruins the piece. A crooked cut cannot be uncut.

So the work Paul commends is not enthusiasm or eloquence but accuracy — taking a text and cutting it straight, giving what is actually there rather than what the preacher would like to be there. And set against the previous verse it is the whole alternative. The word-fighters use Scripture as ammunition; the approved worker handles it like a man who will answer for every cut.

verseByVerse.quote: But avoid irreverent babble, for it will lead people into more and more ungodliness, and their talk will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have swerved from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened. They are upsetting the faith of some.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Avoid irreverent babble.” Not refute it — avoid it. The same instruction as 1 Timothy 6:20, and the same pastoral judgement: some error is not worth the dignity of an argument.

Then the reason, and it is a diagnosis of how error actually behaves: “for it will lead people into more and more ungodliness, and their talk will spread like gangrene.”

Two observations, and both are exact. Error progresses — it does not settle at a tolerable level but leads on, and each position makes the next one thinkable. And it spreads by contact. Gangrene is a medical term, and Paul, who has used the language of sound and diseased teaching throughout these letters, chooses the most unpleasant word available. Gangrene does not stay where it started, cannot be reasoned with, and is treated by cutting away.

Then two names: “Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus.” Hymenaeus appeared in the first letter, handed over to Satan that he might learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim 1:20). He is still at it, and has acquired a colleague. Discipline had been applied and had not worked — which the New Testament records without pretending otherwise.

And their error is specified: “saying that the resurrection has already happened.” Almost certainly a spiritualising of it — that resurrection means the new life a believer has now, and there is nothing bodily still to come. It is an attractive teaching, because it sounds advanced and requires nothing to be waited for.

“They are upsetting the faith of some.” The verb means to overturn — the same idea as the ruin of verse 14. And this is precisely why it matters: if resurrection has already happened, then the Christians whose bodies are in the ground have missed it, and everyone still suffering has nothing coming. It is the identical pastoral wreckage the Thessalonians suffered when told the day had already come (2 Thess 2:2), and both times it landed on the grieving first.

verseByVerse.quote: But God's firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: "The Lord knows those who are his," and, "Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against men who are overturning the faith of some, Paul sets something that cannot be overturned: “God's firm foundation stands.”

The image is a building's foundation stone, and in the ancient world such stones were commonly inscribed. Paul says this one carries a seal with two lines on it — and they face in opposite directions.

The first is God's side: “The Lord knows those who are his.” It is quoted from Numbers 16:5, Moses' answer when Korah's rebellion made it unclear who genuinely belonged to God. That is exactly Timothy's situation — respected teachers have defected, people are unsettled, and nobody is sure who is sound. Paul's answer is that the register is not kept by us. God knows, and his knowledge is not affected by our confusion.

That is a real comfort in a church that has had a scandal. You may not know who is genuine; you may have been badly wrong about somebody. He is not in any doubt.

The second line is our side: “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.” If you cannot verify who belongs to God, you can attend to your own conduct — and the standard is stated as a consequence of the naming. Whoever claims the name is thereby committed to leaving the sin.

Hold the two together and you have the balance the whole New Testament keeps. Assurance rests on God's knowledge, not on our performance — nobody is kept by the quality of their departure from iniquity. And the evidence that a person belongs is precisely that departure. The seal has two lines, and a foundation with only one of them on it will not hold a building up.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honorable use, some for dishonorable. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable, he will be a vessel for honorable use, set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul stays with the house. “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honourable use, some for dishonourable.”

The picture is a large establishment with a range of equipment. Gold and silver for the table; wood and clay for the kitchen, the yard, and the jobs nobody describes at dinner. Every big household had both, and nobody thought this strange.

Applied to the church — the household of God (1 Tim 3:15) — it accounts for what Timothy is looking at. Hymenaeus and Philetus are in the house. Their presence does not mean the house is false; large households contain vessels of very different kinds, and it has always been so.

Then verse 21 makes the turn, and it is the crucial move: “if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonourable, he will be a vessel for honourable use.”

Notice what Paul does not say. He does not tell Timothy to sort the house or identify which people are the clay ones. The instruction is reflexive — cleanse yourself. Faced with a congregation containing frauds, the temptation is to spend your energy on auditing everybody else, and Paul redirects it entirely.

And the promise is remarkable, because it means the classification is not fixed. A vessel can move category. Nobody in this house is stuck being clay, and the transfer is effected by cleansing rather than by gifting or promotion.

Four things follow for such a vessel: “set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work.” The middle one is the plainest ambition in Scripture. Not admired, not prominent — useful. A vessel exists to be picked up and employed by its owner, and the whole point of being clean is that you can be used without spoiling what is put in you.

verseByVerse.quote: So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace.” The same paired verbs as 1 Timothy 6:11, and the same wisdom: run from, and run toward. Avoidance alone leaves a vacuum.

“Youthful passions” is usually heard as sexual, and it certainly includes that — Timothy is a young unmarried man and Paul told him to treat younger women as sisters, in all purity (1 Tim 5:2). But the phrase is wider than that, and the context here points elsewhere. The very next verse is about quarrels. The characteristic passions of a young man also include the appetite for argument, the need to be proved right, impatience, and the ambition to make a mark quickly.

Read that way the verse fits its paragraph exactly. A young minister facing Hymenaeus and Philetus will be tempted to take them on and win — and Paul lists that instinct among the things to run from.

The four to chase are worth their order: righteousness (right dealing), faith, love, and peace — and peace is the pointed one in a chapter about word-fights.

Then the clause that is easy to skip and is the most practical thing in the verse: “along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.”

This is not a solo pursuit. Timothy is to chase these things in company — and the company is specified. Not everyone in the great house; those who call on the Lord from a pure heart. Paul's answer to a young man surrounded by corrosive people is not isolation but better company: find the ones who are genuinely seeking God, and run alongside them.

Anyone who has tried to grow in a difficult church knows how much this matters. You cannot always choose your congregation. You can very largely choose who you spend your time with inside it, and that choice does more to shape a person over ten years than almost anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies; you know that they breed quarrels. And the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth, and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies; you know that they breed quarrels.” The verb for breed is a birth word — controversies do not merely lead to quarrels, they generate them, and they keep doing it.

“You know” is Paul's way of saying this is not a theory. Timothy has watched it happen, and could have predicted the outcome.

Then the portrait of the alternative, and it is one of the finest descriptions of a Christian teacher anywhere: “the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting his opponents with gentleness.”

Take the terms in order. “Not quarrelsome” — the same requirement as an overseer (1 Tim 3:3). “Kind to everyone”, and the scope includes the opponents. “Able to teach” — the one skill on the overseer's list, and note it sits between two dispositions rather than standing alone. “Patiently enduring evil” is a single word meaning to bear ill-treatment without retaliating; it assumes he will be ill-treated.

“Correcting his opponents with gentleness.” Both halves at once. He does correct — this is not a counsel of vagueness, and the word means instructing so as to change someone. And he does it gently. Most of us can manage one or the other.

Then the reason, and it changes the whole temperature: “God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth.”

Repentance is God's to give. That is why gentleness is not weakness or mere good manners — if the outcome depended on the teacher's argument, then overwhelming force would be the sensible tactic. It does not. A man cannot argue anybody into repentance, so his job is to correct clearly, treat people well, and leave the granting to God.

And the last verse says why they need it: “that they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will.” The verb suggests a man sobering up. Paul's picture of his opponents is not that they are villains but that they are caught — taken alive in a trap, held, doing somebody else's will while believing it is their own. That is how he sees the men wrecking his churches, and it is why he tells Timothy to be gentle with them.
