3.title: Perilous Times and the God-Breathed Word
3.overview:
Chapter 3 opens with one of Paul’s most disturbing prophetic passages and closes with one of his most enduring theological affirmations. The juxtaposition is deliberate: the darkness of the description of last-days humanity (vv. 1–9) makes the light of God-breathed Scripture (vv. 16–17) shine all the more brilliantly.

The eighteen vices of vv. 2–5 are a systematic anatomy of godlessness — not paganism but religious godlessness, people who maintain a form of godliness while denying its power. This is the most dangerous kind of false Christianity: externally plausible, internally hollow, and capable of leading astray those who are “always learning but never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth.”

The corrective Paul offers is not a better technique but a deeper anchor: Paul’s own pattern of faith and suffering (vv. 10–12), the solid ground of Scripture received from childhood (vv. 14–15), and the character of Scripture itself as the God-breathed word adequate for everything the minister needs (vv. 16–17). The last-days situation calls not for innovation but for deeper rootedness in what has been given.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Godlessness in the Last Days
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
In the last days there will come times of difficulty (v.1). Paul then lists what people will be: lovers of self and of money, proud, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy (v.2), heartless, unappeasable, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, not loving good (v.3), treacherous, reckless, swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than of God (v.4) — having the appearance of godliness but denying its power. Avoid such people (v.5).

Among them are those who creep into households and capture vulnerable women burdened with sins and led by various passions (v.6), always learning and never arriving at a knowledge of the truth (v.7). As Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these oppose the truth — corrupted in mind, disqualified regarding the faith (v.8). But they will not get far, for their folly will become plain to all, as theirs did (v.9).
verseByVerse.theology:
What 'the Last Days' Means

In New Testament reckoning the last days are not a distant future period; they began with Christ's coming. Peter says so at Pentecost, quoting Joel — this is what was spoken by the prophet, in the last days (Acts 2:16-17) — and Hebrews opens by saying God has spoken to us in these last days by his Son. The whole stretch between resurrection and return is the last days, and Paul and Timothy were living in them. Which is why verse 5 says to avoid such people: you cannot avoid people who will not exist for two thousand years.

The twentieth item is the one that makes the list terrifying. Everything in verses 2-4 could describe the pagan world, and a reader might nod along thinking of the street outside. Then verse 5 puts the whole catalogue inside the church — morphosis, the outline or shape of godliness, maintained while its power is denied. So this is not a description of society at large but of what religion looks like when the power has gone out of it and only the shape is left. And the denial is in the life, not the mouth: these people may recite the creed accurately.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The list is framed by two bookends — 'lovers of self' at the head and 'lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God' at the foot — and everything between is what those two produce. Four items are compounds of philos, lover; it is a list about disordered affection. Note also how little of it concerns false doctrine or outside persecution. It is a portrait of ordinary human relationships coming apart: families, gratitude, natural affection (astorgos), the willingness to accept an apology (aspondos, a treaty word — a person with whom no peace can be made). Not dramatic. Recognisable.

Now: 'Avoid such people' needs its limits. Paul is not describing struggling Christians or people whose lives are a mess — the New Testament is full of instruction about bearing with those. He is describing settled hypocrisy, and his judgement is that such a person is not to be a young minister's project. And the mercy in the passage is verse 9: there is a ceiling. Egypt's magicians kept pace with Moses for two plagues and then could not produce gnats, and had to tell Pharaoh this is the finger of God (Exod 8:18-19). Imitation runs out — usually sooner than the people watching fear.

verseByVerse.quote: But understand this, that in the last days there will come times of difficulty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But understand this, that in the last days there will come times of difficulty.”

The last days in New Testament reckoning are not a distant future period. They began with Christ's coming — Peter says so at Pentecost, quoting Joel: this is what was spoken by the prophet, in the last days (Acts 2:16-17); and Hebrews opens by saying God has spoken to us in these last days by his Son. The whole stretch between the resurrection and the return is the last days, and Paul and Timothy were living in them.

Which is why the very next paragraph tells Timothy to avoid such people (v.5) — you cannot avoid people who will not exist for two thousand years. Paul is describing the conditions of the age Timothy is working in, not a forecast of some remote generation's trouble.

“Times of difficulty.” The word is used only twice in the New Testament, and the other place is striking: Matthew uses it of the two demoniacs among the tombs, so fierce that no one could pass that way (Matt 8:28). It means savage, hard to bear, dangerous. Not merely inconvenient seasons but times with teeth in them.

And note the word Paul chooses for the times themselves: kairoi, appointed seasons. Even the difficult stretches are not random weather. They come, and they belong to a calendar somebody else keeps.

The instruction is simply “understand this” — know it in advance. Paul's consistent pastoral method is to tell people what is coming so that when it arrives it confirms the teaching rather than contradicting it. He did the same at Thessalonica (1 Thess 3:4). A Christian who has been told to expect savage times is not destroyed by them; a Christian promised an easy road is.

verseByVerse.quote: For people will be lovers of self, lovers of money, proud, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, unappeasable, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, not loving good, treacherous, reckless, swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nineteen items in three verses, and the list is framed by two of them. It opens with “lovers of self” and closes with “lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God” — and everything between is what those two produce.

That framing is the whole diagnosis. Paul does not begin with atheism or idolatry. He begins with the self turned inward, and treats the rest as symptoms. The Greek makes it visible: four of the items are compounds of philos, lover — lovers of self, lovers of money, lovers of pleasure, and (negatively) not lovers of good. It is a list about disordered affection.

“Lovers of money” follows immediately, as it does everywhere in these letters (1 Tim 6:10). Then the outward pride: proud, arrogant, abusive — literally blasphemers, people whose speech tears others down.

Then the relational collapse, and this is the heart of the list. “Disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, unappeasable.” Astorgos, heartless, means without natural affection — the failure of the love that ordinarily binds a family without anyone having to try. And aspondos, unappeasable, is a treaty word: literally without libation, refusing the truce. A person with whom no peace can be made, who will not accept an apology.

Then the loss of restraint — “without self-control, brutal” — and finally the betrayals: “treacherous, reckless, swollen with conceit.” The last is the inflation word again (1 Tim 3:6), puffed up with air.

Read the whole run and notice what it is not. There is scarcely anything here about false doctrine, and nothing about persecution from outside. It is a portrait of ordinary human relationships coming apart — families, gratitude, affection, promises, self-restraint — and Paul says this is what the difficult times will actually look like. Not dramatic. Recognisable.

verseByVerse.quote: having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power. Avoid such people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then the twentieth item, which is the one that makes the list terrifying: “having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power.”

Everything in verses 2-4 could describe the pagan world, and a reader might have nodded along thinking of Ephesus outside the door. This last clause puts the whole catalogue inside the church.

The word for appearance is morphosis — an outline, a form, the shape of a thing. These are people with the recognisable outline of religion. They attend, they use the vocabulary, they would be offended to be told they were not Christians. What is missing is power — dynamis, the thing that actually changes people.

So the list is not a description of society at large. It is a description of what religion looks like when the power has gone out of it and only the shape remains. A self-loving, money-loving, ungrateful, unappeasable man who is also at church every week — that is the figure Paul is warning about.

“Denying its power.” Not denying doctrine. These people may well recite the creed accurately. What they deny, in practice, is that godliness does anything — and the denial is in the life, not the mouth. Which is exactly what the letter has been saying since 1 Timothy 1:5: teaching is measured by what it produces.

Then the instruction, and it is short: “Avoid such people.” Turn away from them. Not argue them down, not reform them — the same counsel as 2:16 about irreverent babble.

It is a hard word and it needs its limits. Paul is not describing struggling Christians or people whose lives are a mess; the New Testament is full of instruction about bearing with those. He is describing settled hypocrisy — the outline of godliness maintained deliberately over a life that denies it — and his judgement is that such people are not to be Timothy's project. There is a kind of person a young minister can pour years into and have nothing to show, and Paul tells him not to.

verseByVerse.quote: For among them are those who creep into households and capture weak women, burdened with sins and led astray by various passions, always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now says what these people actually do, and it is predatory. “Among them are those who creep into households and capture weak women.”

The first verb means to worm in, to insinuate oneself — entry by stealth rather than invitation. And “capture” is a war word: to take captive, to lead away as a prisoner. It is the same picture as 2:26, where people are caught alive in the devil's snare.

The target is households, which is where the churches met and where the women of that world spent their days. A man with religious credentials could get into a home in a way he could never get into a synagogue or a public gathering.

“Weak women” is a diminutive in Greek and it is not kind; it carries a note of contempt. But note carefully whose contempt it is. Paul is not sneering at women as such — this is the man who names Lois and Eunice as the source of Timothy's faith two paragraphs later, and who lists women as fellow workers everywhere he goes. He is describing particular people who were being exploited, and the description that follows is of vulnerability rather than stupidity: “burdened with sins and led astray by various passions.”

That is the profile of the target, and it is the profile predators have always looked for: someone carrying guilt, and someone whose desires are pulling in several directions at once. A person weighed down by things they have done and cannot resolve will listen to anybody who offers relief.

“Always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth.” It is one of the saddest phrases in the New Testament and it describes the effect rather than the appetite. These women are not idle; they are studying. But the teaching they are being fed is the endless kind Paul described in the first letter — speculation that never lands (1 Tim 1:4). Perpetual learning that never arrives is not a failure of effort. It is what a certain kind of teaching is designed to produce, because a person who arrives no longer needs the teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth, men corrupted in mind and disqualified regarding the faith. But they will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all, as was that of those two men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth.” The names are not in the Old Testament. They come from Jewish tradition, which gave them to the magicians of Pharaoh's court who duplicated Moses' signs before Aaron's staff swallowed theirs (Exod 7:11-12).

Paul is using a tradition his readers knew, as he uses Greek poets elsewhere, and the choice of comparison is exact. The Egyptian magicians did not deny Moses or argue with him. They reproduced what he did. Their opposition was imitation — which is precisely the danger of men who have the outline of godliness (v.5).

“Men corrupted in mind and disqualified regarding the faith.” The second word is adokimos — the assayer's word again, and this time in the negative: metal tested and rejected. Timothy is to present himself approved (2:15); these men are the failed assay, and the two verses are meant to be read against each other.

Then the limit, and it is the mercy in the passage: “But they will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all.”

That is a genuine encouragement to a man watching a church being damaged. Paul does not promise the trouble will be brief or painless — Hymenaeus was still going in chapter 2 after being disciplined in the first letter. He promises there is a ceiling. This kind of thing exposes itself in the end, and the exposure comes from the folly's own nature rather than from anyone's campaign against it.

“As was that of those two men.” Egypt's magicians kept pace with Moses through the first two plagues and then could not produce gnats, and had to tell Pharaoh this is the finger of God (Exod 8:18-19). Imitation runs out. It always does, and usually sooner than the people watching fear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Scripture and the Man of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Timothy, by contrast, has followed Paul's teaching, conduct, aim in life, faith, patience, love and steadfastness (v.10), and his persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra — from all of which the Lord rescued him (v.11). Indeed all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (v.12), while evil people and impostors go on from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived (v.13).

So Timothy is to continue in what he has learned and firmly believed, knowing from whom he learned it (v.14), and how from infancy he has known the sacred writings, which are able to make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (v.15). All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, reproof, correction and training in righteousness (v.16), so that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work (v.17).
verseByVerse.theology:
Breathed Out by God

Theopneustos occurs nowhere else in the Greek Bible and Paul may have coined it: theos, God, and pneo, to breathe. Note the direction — not God-inbreathed, as though he blew life into documents that already existed, but God-outbreathed. Scripture proceeds from him as breath proceeds from a speaker. The older word 'inspired' has drifted, and now suggests a heightened human state — we call a poem inspired. The claim is about origin, not about the writers' elevated feelings.

Nor does it mean dictation. Luke researched (Luke 1:3), Paul argues and occasionally loses his temper, David bleeds all over the Psalms; the writers' personalities and circumstances are everywhere in the text. Peter puts both halves together: men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Pet 1:21) — genuinely speaking, genuinely carried.

The four uses come in two pairs and the pattern is exact: Scripture tells you what is true (teaching), shows you where you are wrong (reproof), puts you back on your feet (correction — the word means setting upright again), and then trains you over years (the word is the one for raising a child). It does not stop at diagnosis. A reader who only ever feels rebuked by the Bible is using half of it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The three towns in verse 11 are not chosen at random. They are the towns of the first missionary journey (Acts 13-14), and Lystra is Timothy's home (Acts 16:1). At Antioch Paul was driven out; at Iconium they tried to stone him; at Lystra they succeeded and dragged him out of the city supposing he was dead (Acts 14:19). Paul is reminding Timothy of something he very likely saw as a boy — a man stoned and left for dead who got up and went back into the city. And 'from them all the Lord rescued me' is written by a man who knows he will not be rescued this time; the rescue is not cancelled by the execution but completed by it (4:18).

Now: Verse 12 must be read honestly rather than dramatically. Most Christians in comfortable countries will not be imprisoned, and pretending otherwise cheapens the word for those who are. But persecution has a wide range, and its ordinary end is recognisable: the family that finds you embarrassing, the promotion your convictions cost you, friendships that quietly cool. Note too that the trigger is desire — those who want to live a godly life — so nobody escapes by concluding they are not godly enough to qualify. And the verse settles a question people ask when things go badly: opposition for godliness is not evidence of failure. Its absence is the thing worth examining.

verseByVerse.quote: You, however, have followed my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness, my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra—which persecutions I endured; yet from them all the Lord rescued me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You, however, have followed my teaching” — the pronoun is emphatic and turns the chapter. Against the imitators who have the shape of godliness, one young man who has had the real thing in front of him for years.

The verb means to follow closely, to accompany — the word for a disciple keeping pace with a teacher. And what follows is a list of nine things, and it repays reading slowly, because of what stands where.

“My teaching” comes first, and then everything else is life: “my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness, my persecutions and sufferings.” One item of doctrine and eight of character and circumstance.

That proportion is the point. Timothy did not learn Paul chiefly in a lecture. He learned him on the road — how he behaved, what he was aiming at, how he took it when things went wrong. “My aim in life” is a single word meaning purpose or resolve, the thing a man is actually for. Timothy had watched Paul long enough to know what that was.

Then three named places: “at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra.” These are not chosen at random. They are the towns of the first missionary journey (Acts 13-14) — and Lystra is Timothy's home town (Acts 16:1). At Antioch Paul was driven out; at Iconium they tried to stone him; at Lystra they succeeded, and dragged him out of the city supposing he was dead (Acts 14:19).

So Paul is reminding Timothy of something he very likely saw. A boy in Lystra watching a man stoned and left for dead, who got up and went back into the city. That is where this young man's discipleship began, and Paul is telling him to remember it now that the price has come due again.

“Yet from them all the Lord rescued me.” Written from a cell by a man who knows he will not be rescued this time — and he says it anyway, because it is true. The rescues were real. That God does not always rescue does not mean he never does, and Paul will say in the next chapter that the Lord will bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom (4:18). The rescue is not cancelled by the execution; it is completed by it.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, while evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.”

It is one of the flattest, least qualified sentences in the New Testament. Not some. Not those in hostile places. All — and the promise is not of hardship in general but of opposition, from people, because of godliness.

Note the phrasing: those who desire to live a godly life. The trigger is not achievement but intention. It is the wanting that draws fire, which means nobody can escape by concluding they are not godly enough to qualify.

And it must be read honestly rather than dramatically. Most Christians in comfortable countries are not going to be imprisoned, and pretending otherwise cheapens the word for those who are. But persecution has always had a wide range, and its ordinary end is recognisable enough: the family that finds you embarrassing, the workplace where your convictions cost you the promotion, the friendships that quietly cool, being thought narrow or unintelligent. Paul's word covers the whole spectrum, and the mild end of it is where most readers will meet it.

The verse also settles a question people ask when things go badly: have I done something wrong? Opposition for godliness is not evidence of failure. It is what the text says to expect, and its absence is the thing that might be worth examining.

Then the parallel movement in verse 13: “evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse.” The word for impostor is literally a wailer or enchanter — a sorcerer, which reaches back to Jannes and Jambres in verse 8.

“Deceiving and being deceived.” Both at once, and the order matters. The deceiver is himself deceived, and the two feed each other — a man who tells people what is not true for long enough stops being able to tell. It is one of the more frightening observations in Scripture, because it means the state Paul is describing is not one its occupant can detect from inside.

So the two verses run in opposite directions at once. The godly are pressed, and the impostors advance. Paul sets them side by side without softening either, and then tells Timothy what to do about it.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it and how from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But as for you” — the contrast again, and now the instruction: “continue in what you have learned and have firmly believed.”

The verb means to remain, to stay put. Against a world going from bad to worse, Timothy is not told to innovate or to devise a strategy. He is told to stay where he is. In a chapter about people who are always learning and never arriving, that is a deliberate counter-instruction.

Then two reasons, and they are the two grounds on which anyone holds the faith.

The first is personal: “knowing from whom you learned it.” The pronoun is plural in the best reading — from what persons. Paul, certainly; but the next verse names the others, and the plural has already been filled in at 1:5 with Lois and Eunice. Timothy is to weigh the teaching against the people it came through. He watched them. He knows what it made of them.

That is not an argument from authority but from evidence, and it is one most Christians actually use. When doctrine is under pressure, part of what steadies a person is the recollection of specific believers whose lives could not be explained any other way.

The second reason is the text itself: “how from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings.” The word for childhood means infancy — from the cradle.

Here is where the chapter's threads meet. The “sacred writings” are the Old Testament, and Timothy's father was a Greek (Acts 16:1), so the teaching came from his mother and grandmother. Two women taught a small boy the Scriptures, and forty years later Paul points to it as the reason he will hold when everyone else defects.

“Which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.” Note the qualifier. The Old Testament made Timothy wise for salvation — but through faith in Christ. Scripture does not save by being read; it makes wise unto salvation by pointing to someone. Take the pointing away and you have a man who knows the sacred writings very well and is not saved by them, which describes a good many of Paul's opponents.

verseByVerse.quote: All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“All Scripture is breathed out by God.”

The word is theopneustos, and Paul may well have coined it — theos, God, and pneo, to breathe. It occurs nowhere else in the Greek Bible. And note the direction: not God-inbreathed, as though he blew life into documents that already existed, but God-outbreathed. Scripture proceeds from him the way breath proceeds from a speaker.

The older translation “inspired” has drifted and now suggests a heightened human state — we call a poem or a performance inspired. That is not the claim. The claim is about origin, not about the elevated feelings of the writers.

And it does not mean dictation. Luke researched (Luke 1:3), Paul argues and occasionally loses his temper, David bleeds all over the Psalms. The writers' personalities, vocabularies and circumstances are everywhere in the text. Peter puts both halves together: men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Pet 1:21) — genuinely speaking, genuinely carried.

“All Scripture.” Not the parts that move you, not the parts a modern reader finds congenial. The genealogies, the building specifications, the imprecatory psalms. Paul's immediate reference is the Old Testament — the sacred writings of verse 15 — which should be stressed, because it is the part of the Bible Christians most often quietly shelve.

Then the purpose, and Paul gives four uses in two pairs. “Teaching” — what is true. “Reproof” — where you are wrong. “Correction” — the word means setting upright again, restoring to a proper state. “Training in righteousness” — and the word is the one for raising a child, the long formation of somebody over years.

The pattern is exact and every Christian should know it: Scripture tells you the truth, shows you where you are wrong, puts you back on your feet, and then trains you. It does not stop at diagnosis. A reader who only ever feels rebuked by the Bible is using half of it.

And the goal in verse 17: “that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.” The title is the prophet's title from 1 Timothy 6:11. Complete means fitted, finished, up to the job. And equipped is a word for having been fully furnished with tools.

That is the answer to the whole chapter. Savage times, imitators with the outline of godliness, predators in households, deceivers going from bad to worse — and what Timothy is handed against all of it is a book. Not a technique, not a strategy, not secret knowledge. Paul's last substantial word to his successor is that the Scriptures are sufficient to make a man complete and furnish him for everything he will be asked to do.

Avoid such people.<sup>6</sup>For among them are those who creep into households and capture weak women, burdened with sins and led astray by various passions,<sup>7</sup>always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth.<sup>8</sup>Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth, men corrupted in mind and disqualified regarding the faith.<sup>9</sup>But they will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all, as was that of those two men.<sup>10</sup>You, however, have followed my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness,<sup>11</sup>my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra—which persecutions I endured; yet from them all the Lord rescued me.<sup>12</sup>Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted,<sup>13</sup>while evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.<sup>14</sup>But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it<sup>15</sup>and how from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.<sup>16</sup>All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness,<sup>17</sup>that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.

4.title: Preach the Word: The Commission, the Crown, and the Cloak
4.overview:
The final chapter of 2 Timothy is Paul’s most personal and most urgent. He has told Timothy what the gospel is, what the minister must do, what Scripture provides, and what opposition to expect. Now he gives the direct commission — preach the word — and then, with the unsentimental clarity of a man who can see the end of the road, he describes where that commission has brought him: not to triumph but to the threshold of death, with a faithful conscience and an unflinching confidence in the one who has been his judge all along.

The charge of vv. 1–8 is the most solemn in the Pauline corpus. The invocation of God and Christ Jesus as witnesses, the eschatological framework of the appearing and the kingdom, the urgency of “in season and out of season” — these are not administrative instructions; they are the last words of a man who has paid every cost the commission demanded and now calls his successor to pay the same.

The final section (vv. 9–22) is the most humanly moving passage Paul ever wrote. The request for the cloak and the books. The notice of Demas’s defection — devastating in its compression. “Only Luke is with me.” The greetings sent and received. The final benediction: “The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.” Paul has written great theology; but he ends with a cloak, a few friends, and the grace of Christ. It is enough.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Preach the Word, and Finish the Race
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul charges Timothy before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom (v.1): preach the word, be ready in season and out, reprove, rebuke and exhort, with complete patience and teaching (v.2). For a time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching but, with itching ears, will heap up teachers to suit their own passions (v.3), turning from the truth and wandering into myths (v.4). Timothy is to stay sober-minded, endure suffering, do an evangelist's work, and fulfil his ministry (v.5).

For Paul is already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of his departure has come (v.6). He has fought the good fight, finished the race, kept the faith (v.7); henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for him, to be awarded by the Lord, the righteous judge, on that day — and not to him only but to all who have loved his appearing (v.8).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Last Charge, and the Steward's Report

Every element of the oath in verse 1 is chosen. Paul is about to be judged by a Roman court, and he swears Timothy by a different one — whose jurisdiction covers the living and the dead, which means it will have both Paul and Nero in front of it.

Verse 7's three clauses are all in the Greek perfect: completed, with the result standing. And it is not a boast, which matters. The man who wrote that grace was given before the ages began and not because of works (1:9), and who called himself the foremost of sinners, has removed any possibility of reading it as self-congratulation. It is a steward's report. Note too that he does not claim to have won every engagement — he says the contest itself was good, worth entering. And 'I have kept the faith' uses the guarding word: after a letter built on the deposit, he can report that it is intact.

Then verse 8 opens outward, and this is why the passage belongs to every reader. The crown is 'not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.' The qualification is not apostleship or martyrdom or a comparable race. It is longing for Christ to come — a settled affection, and a fair test of where a person's treasure is, since a man tells you what he loves by what he hopes is coming.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verse 3 locates the problem on the demand side, which is unusual and uncomfortable — we generally blame bad teachers for bad churches. The itch is in the hearers' ears, and they 'accumulate for themselves' a pile of teachers chosen to suit their passions. These are not people misled by a teacher who arrived; they assembled a collection. And verse 4's two movements are one motion: nobody stops at turning away, because a person who stops listening to the truth does not become neutral — there is always something to drift into.

Now: Anyone can now assemble a set of teachers who agree with him more easily than at any point in history, and can do it while believing he is being discerning. The test is not whether you like your teachers but whether you can remember the last time one of them told you something you did not want to hear. Note also the balance of verse 2: reprove and rebuke are hard words and exhort is a warm one, and a ministry with only the first two is a bludgeon while one with only the third is a comfortable fraud — all of it governed by patience and teaching, since reproof without instruction leaves a man knowing he is wrong and not knowing what is right.

verseByVerse.quote: I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most solemn charge in the letters, and every element of the oath is chosen. “In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom.”

Paul is about to be judged by a Roman court. He swears Timothy by a different court — one whose jurisdiction covers the living and the dead, which is to say it will have both Paul and Nero in front of it.

Then the charge itself, in nine short imperatives that come like hammer blows.

“Preach the word.” The verb is the herald's — to announce publicly what someone else has given you to say. A herald does not compose his message or improve it; he delivers it. And the object is definite: the word, the deposit, not the preacher's own thoughts about it.

“Be ready in season and out of season.” Literally: be at hand when it is convenient and when it is not. The phrase concedes that there will be plenty of the second kind, and instructs him to be standing by anyway.

Then three verbs covering the range of what preaching does. “Reprove” — to convict, to show a man he is wrong. “Rebuke” — the sharper word, censure. “Exhort” — parakaleo, to call alongside, encourage, comfort. Two hard and one warm, and a ministry with only the first two is a bludgeon while one with only the third is a comfortable fraud.

And then the two qualifiers that govern all of it: “with complete patience and teaching.” Patience because people change slowly, and the word is the long-tempered one, slow to take offence. Teaching because reproof without instruction leaves a man knowing he is wrong and not knowing what is right.

Put together, this is the whole job description. Announce what you were given, be available whether or not it suits, tell people the truth including the parts they dislike, encourage them — and do it all slowly and with explanation.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions, and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now gives the reason the charge is so heavy, and it is not that people will attack the truth. It is that they will lose their appetite for it.

“They will not endure sound teaching.” The verb means to put up with, to tolerate. The problem is not that healthy teaching is refuted but that it becomes unbearable — and sound is the medical word again, wholesome, the diet that keeps a body well.

“But having itching ears.” The image is of ears that want to be scratched. Note where the itch is: in the hearers, not the teachers. Paul locates the demand side first, which is unusual and uncomfortable, because we generally blame bad teachers for bad churches. He says the market comes before the supply.

“They will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions.” The verb means to heap up — a pile of teachers, which suggests both quantity and choice. And the criterion is stated without embarrassment: to suit their own passions. They will select for agreement.

The phrase “for themselves” is doing quiet work. These are not people who were misled by a teacher who arrived; they went out and assembled a collection. The passivity we normally assume in such situations is not in the text.

Then the two movements of verse 4, and they are one motion: they “turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths.” Nobody stops at the turning away. A person who stops listening to the truth does not become neutral; the second verb is the drifting one, and there is always something to drift into.

In honesty, this describes a temptation nobody is outside of. Anyone can now assemble a set of teachers who agree with him, more easily than at any point in history, and can do it while believing he is being discerning. The test in the verse is not whether you like your teachers but whether you can remember the last time one of them told you something you did not want to hear.

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, always be sober-minded, endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“As for you” — the contrast that has run through these letters, and four final imperatives.

“Always be sober-minded.” The word means clear-headed, self-possessed, unintoxicated. In a church where people are accumulating teachers to scratch their ears, Timothy is to keep his head. It is not a glamorous instruction and it is the first one.

“Endure suffering.” The same root as the sharing in suffering of 1:8 and 2:3, and by now it has been said so often that Timothy cannot claim he was not told.

“Do the work of an evangelist.” The word means a bringer of good news, and it occurs only three times in the New Testament. Timothy's job in Ephesus was largely corrective — assessing elders, silencing false teachers, managing a widows' roll — and it would be easy for such a man to spend his whole ministry on maintenance. Paul tells him to keep announcing the good news to people who have not heard it. Note the word work: it is a task to be done rather than a gift some possess.

“Fulfil your ministry.” Literally: fill it full, carry it out to the end — the same charge Paul sent to Archippus (Col 4:17). And your ministry, not Paul's. Timothy is not being asked to replace the apostle or to be a second Paul. He has his own commission, and the instruction is to finish it.

These are the last commands Paul ever gave in writing, and there is nothing extraordinary in them. Keep your head, accept the cost, keep telling people the good news, and finish what you were given. A dying apostle's final instruction is not a grand vision but a short list any Christian could be handed.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come.” The reason for the four commands: Timothy must fulfil his ministry because Paul has finished his.

The drink offering was the wine poured over a sacrifice already burning — the last act, the smallest quantity, completing an offering someone else had brought. Paul used the same image from an earlier prison, where it was still hypothetical: even if I am to be poured out (Phil 2:17). Here the conditional is gone. It is happening now, in the present tense.

“The time of my departure.” The word is analysis — the noun matching the verb of Philippians 1:23. Its ordinary uses are all of journeys ending: untying a ship from the quay, striking a tent, loosing an animal from the yoke, freeing a prisoner from his chains. Every one implies somewhere to go, and Paul chooses it deliberately for what is about to happen to him under a Roman sword.

“Has come” is a nautical and military word too — it is used of a ship's arrival and of the moment something is at hand. He is not speculating about the future. The thing is here.

And note the word already. Paul does not say he is about to be poured out; the pouring has started. Whatever the legal position, in his own reckoning the offering is under way — which is a striking thing for a man to conclude about his own last months while he is still alive to write about them.

The whole image also reclassifies what is being done to him. Rome believes it is disposing of a troublesome provincial. Paul describes a priest at an altar. He is not being executed; he is being poured — and the offering is not his own but one that someone else is already burning.

What is remarkable is the composure of the sentence. There is no panic in it and no resignation either. A man writing weeks or months from execution reaches for the language of the altar and of a boat casting off, and then in the next breath asks Timothy to bring his coat.

verseByVerse.quote: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three clauses, all in the same tense — the Greek perfect, which describes something completed whose result stands. Not “I fought and it is over” but “I have fought, and it is done.”

“I have fought the good fight.” The words are cognate: I have contended the good contest, from the arena. It is the same charge he gave Timothy in the first letter (1 Tim 6:12) and in 2:5 here — and Paul can now report it in the past tense about himself. Note the adjective: the fight was good. He does not say he won every engagement. He says the contest itself was worth entering.

“I have finished the race.” The word for race is dromos, a course with a marked end. Paul had used it decades earlier at Miletus, telling the Ephesian elders he only wanted to finish his course and the ministry he received from the Lord (Acts 20:24). He wanted one thing, for years, and here at the end he can say he got it.

“I have kept the faith.” The verb is the guarding word — the same idea as the deposit of 1:14. And the phrase can be read two ways, both true: he has kept faith, as one keeps a promise or an oath; and he has kept the faith, the body of truth entrusted to him. Given how this letter has hammered the deposit, the second is surely primary.

What the verse is not is a boast, and the reason should be clear. Paul has just written that grace was given before the ages began and not because of works (1:9), and he called himself the foremost of sinners in the first letter. A man who has said those things has removed any possibility of reading this as self-congratulation. It is a steward's report, not a claim.

And it is a rare and precious thing that anyone should be able to say it. Most people arrive at the end with things unfinished and are not sure what they were for. Paul knew exactly what he had been given to do, did it, and could say so without either false modesty or pride. That is the fruit of a life with one aim in it (3:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness.” The word means from now on — the settled state of affairs from this point. And “laid up” means reserved, stored, put by for someone. It is already there, waiting, with his name on it.

“The crown” is stephanos, the victor's wreath at the games rather than a royal diadem — the athletic image running to its end. And “of righteousness” most likely means the crown that consists of righteousness: the thing awarded is being finally and fully right with God, which is what Paul spent his life insisting could not be earned.

“Which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day.” Set that against the setting. Paul is awaiting the verdict of a Roman court which will find against him. He looks past it to a different bench, and calls that judge righteous — which is precisely what the one in Rome is not.

There is real comfort here for anyone who has been treated unjustly and can do nothing about it. Paul does not deny the injustice or minimise it. He appeals it to a higher court, and waits.

Then the clause that opens the whole thing outward, and it is the reason this verse belongs to every Christian: “and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.”

The crown is not a special award for apostles or martyrs. The qualification is stated, and it is startlingly simple: those who have loved his appearing — who have longed for Christ to come, and wanted it. Not those who fought the good fight as Paul did, or finished a comparable race. Those who loved the thought of seeing him.

The tense is perfect again: have loved, and go on loving. It is a settled affection, and it is a fair test of where a person's treasure is. A man tells you what he loves by what he hopes is coming.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Come soon (v.9) — for Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted him for Thessalonica; Crescens has gone to Galatia and Titus to Dalmatia (v.10). Luke alone is with him; bring Mark, who is useful for ministry (v.11); Tychicus has been sent to Ephesus (v.12). Bring the cloak left with Carpus at Troas, and the books, above all the parchments (v.13).

Alexander the coppersmith did him great harm, and the Lord will repay him (v.14); Timothy should beware of him, for he strongly opposed the message (v.15). At Paul's first defence nobody stood by him and all deserted him — may it not be charged against them (v.16). But the Lord stood by him and strengthened him, so that the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles hear it, and he was rescued from the lion's mouth (v.17). The Lord will rescue him from every evil deed and bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom; to him be glory for ever (v.18).

Greetings to Prisca and Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus (v.19); Erastus stayed at Corinth, and Trophimus was left ill at Miletus (v.20). Come before winter; Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia and all the brothers send greetings (v.21). The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you (v.22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kinds of Wrong, Two Different Prayers

Set verse 14 beside verse 16 and Paul is doing something precise. Of Alexander, who did him great harm and may well have informed on him, he says only that the Lord will repay — a plain future in the better manuscripts, not the curse the older versions suggest. He does not minimise the injury, does not produce a strained forgiveness that denies the damage, and does not retaliate or ask God to retaliate for him. He hands the account over, which is exactly what he taught (Rom 12:19).

But of the friends who abandoned him at his hearing he prays actively: may it not be charged against them. He distinguishes cowardice from malice and treats them differently. And that prayer is Stephen's, as the stones came in (Acts 7:60) — which Paul heard while holding the coats. Thirty years later, deserted himself, he prays the prayer he once watched a dying man pray.

Note also what verse 18 claims and does not claim. 'The Lord will rescue me' is written by a man who knows he will not be spared; the rescue he expects runs through the execution and into the kingdom. That is Christian confidence at close range — not that nothing bad will happen, but that nothing bad can finally prevent the arrival.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Demas was an insider, greeted alongside Luke in Col 4:14 and Philem 24, and the charge against him is not heresy or scandal: he fell in love with this present age. That is how most people leave — not with a repudiation but a preference, something ordinary and legitimate becoming more attractive than a chained old man in Rome. Against him stands Mark, whom Paul had once refused to travel with after he abandoned the mission (Acts 15:37-39), and who is now sent for by name as 'very useful'. Barnabas was right, and Paul says so without defensiveness or revisiting the argument. Grace restores the failed — and the people who gave up on them.

Now: Verse 13 is one of the most humanising verses in Scripture, five verses after the crown of righteousness: the same man thinks about eternity and about being cold. He wants his cloak, and 'above all the parchments' — a man weeks from execution sending across the empire for something to read. William Tyndale, in a cell at Vilvoorde awaiting the same end, asked the governor for a warmer cap, a woollen shirt, and above all his Hebrew Bible, grammar and dictionary; he was almost certainly quoting this verse. Note too v.20: Paul left Trophimus behind ill. The apostle through whom God did extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11) did not heal his friend — one of the plainest proofs that healing was never a technique the apostles could operate at will.

verseByVerse.quote: Do your best to come to me soon. For Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry. Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do your best to come to me soon.” After the crown and the righteous judge, this. The greatest missionary in history, having just written one of the noblest passages in Scripture, asks a young man to hurry up and visit. He is lonely.

Then the reason, and it is a roll-call of absence. “Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me.” We met Demas twice before, sending greetings alongside Luke in Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 24 — an insider, one of the circle. And the charge is not heresy or scandal. He fell in love with this present age.

That is how most people leave, and it should be said plainly. Not with a repudiation but with a preference. Something ordinary and legitimate — comfort, safety, a quieter life — became more attractive than a chained old man in Rome. Nobody would have accused Demas of anything at the time.

“Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia.” No blame attaches to these two; they are on assignment. But the effect on Paul is the same as if they had deserted. The room is empty either way.

“Luke alone is with me.” Three words, and after a chapter of names they are worth stopping on. The physician of Colossians 4:14 is still there at the end — the man who travelled with Paul through the shipwreck and wrote the account of it, sitting in a Roman cell when everyone else has gone.

Then a sentence that is one of the loveliest in the New Testament for what it does not say: “Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry.”

This is the John Mark who abandoned Paul mid-journey and caused so sharp a disagreement with Barnabas that the two men parted (Acts 15:37-39). Paul had refused to take him. Here, at the end of everything, he sends for him — and the word he uses is useful, which is what Onesimus's name means and what Paul asked Philemon to see in another failed man.

Barnabas was right, and Paul says so by sending for him. There is no defensiveness in it and no revisiting of the old argument. A man who once wrote a colleague off asks for him by name in his final letter, and tradition holds that Mark wrote the second Gospel. Grace restores the failed, and it also restores the people who gave up on them.

verseByVerse.quote: When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, also the books, and above all the parchments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, also the books, and above all the parchments.”

It is one of the most humanising verses in the Bible, and it comes five verses after the crown of righteousness. The same man, in the same paragraph, thinks about eternity and about being cold.

The cloak was a heavy circular travelling garment, expensive, the kind of thing a poor man owned one of. He left it at Troas — probably in a hurried arrest — and a Roman prison in winter is a serious matter for a man in his sixties. He asks Timothy to come before winter (v.21), and this is why.

Then “the books, and above all the parchments.” The books are papyrus rolls; the parchments are vellum, more durable and far more expensive — most likely portions of the Old Testament Scriptures, possibly his own notes or legal documents. Whatever they were, he wanted them enough to say above all.

Consider what that means. A man who has written that he has finished the race, weeks or months from execution, sends across the empire for something to read. He is not winding down. He wants his books, and he wants the Scriptures most.

William Tyndale, in a cell at Vilvoorde and about to be strangled and burned, wrote to the governor asking for a warmer cap, a woollen shirt, and above all his Hebrew Bible, grammar and dictionary. He was almost certainly quoting this verse deliberately. It is one of the great echoes in church history, and it shows how exactly one prisoner understood another.

The verse also quietly refutes a certain kind of spirituality. Paul is not too heavenly minded to be cold. Faith of the sort this letter describes does not float above the body's needs or pretend they are beneath notice; it asks for a coat.

verseByVerse.quote: Alexander the coppersmith did me great harm; the Lord will repay him according to his deeds. Beware of him yourself, for he strongly opposed our message.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Alexander the coppersmith did me great harm.” We are not told what he did. The word for harm is strong — he showed Paul much evil — and given the setting it may well be that Alexander informed on him, which would make him the reason Paul is in this cell.

“The Lord will repay him according to his deeds.” Read the tense carefully, because the older translations render it as a wish — may the Lord repay him — and the better manuscripts have a plain future. Paul is not cursing. He is stating what will happen, and leaving it there.

The distinction matters enormously. Paul has been badly injured by this man and does not pretend otherwise, does not say it was nothing, does not produce a strained forgiveness that denies the damage. He also does not retaliate, and he does not ask God to retaliate on his behalf. He hands the account over.

That is exactly what he taught: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, vengeance is mine, I will repay (Rom 12:19). The reason a Christian can let an injury go is not that it did not matter but that it will be dealt with by someone better placed to do it.

And note the contrast with the very next verse. Of the friends who abandoned him at his trial Paul prays, may it not be charged against them — active intercession for their forgiveness. Of Alexander he says only that the Lord will repay. He distinguishes between cowardice and malice, and treats them differently.

“Beware of him yourself, for he strongly opposed our message.” The warning is practical rather than bitter. Timothy will be travelling to Rome, and Paul tells him there is a dangerous man in the way. Forgiveness never required anybody to be naive, and warning a young colleague about a person who has proved dangerous is not gossip but protection.

verseByVerse.quote: At my first defense no one came to stand by me, but all deserted me. May it not be charged against them! But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it. So I was rescued from the lion's mouth. The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“At my first defence no one came to stand by me, but all deserted me.” The phrase is a legal one — the first hearing of his case, where a defendant would ordinarily be supported by friends prepared to speak for his character. Paul had none. Every one of them stayed away.

“May it not be charged against them!” It is the only response he makes, and it is Stephen's prayer as the stones came in — Lord, do not hold this sin against them (Acts 7:60) — which Paul heard, standing there approving, while he held the coats. Thirty years later, deserted himself, he prays the prayer he once watched a dying man pray.

He does not excuse them. It was a sin; that is why it might be charged. He simply asks that it not be.

“But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me.” The verb is the one the friends did not do — nobody stood by him, and then the Lord did. It is a deliberate echo, and it is the whole comfort of the passage. The support Paul was owed and did not get was supplied by someone else, in the same room, at the same hour.

And the purpose is characteristic: not that Paul might be acquitted, but “so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it.” He was strengthened in order to preach — in a Roman court, at his own capital trial, to whoever was in the room. He has spent his life saying he was appointed apostle to the Gentiles, and his defence hearing became the last venue for it.

“So I was rescued from the lion's mouth.” Probably a proverbial phrase for extreme danger, drawn from the Psalms (Ps 22:21). Whatever the immediate reference, the hearing did not end in sentence — he lived to write this letter.

Then verse 18, and note precisely what he claims: “The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom.” He does not say he will be delivered from death; he knows he will not be. The rescue he expects is through the execution and into the kingdom. That is what Christian confidence actually looks like at close range — not the assurance that nothing bad will happen, but that nothing bad can finally prevent the arrival. And so his last doxology: to him be the glory for ever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth, and I left Trophimus, who was ill, at Miletus. Do your best to come before winter. Eubulus sends greetings to you, as do Pudens and Linus and Claudia and all the brothers. The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last words we have from Paul are greetings, and they repay reading slowly, because of who is in them.

“Greet Prisca and Aquila.” The couple he met in Corinth when they had been expelled from Rome, tentmakers like himself, who took Apollos aside and explained the way of God more accurately, and who once risked their necks for his life (Acts 18:2-3, 26; Rom 16:3-4). Thirty years of friendship, and he names the wife first, as he usually does.

“And the household of Onesiphorus.” The man who searched Rome until he found him (1:16-18). Paul greets the household rather than the man, which many take to mean he had since died.

Then two men left behind: “Erastus remained at Corinth, and I left Trophimus, who was ill, at Miletus.” The second is quietly significant. Paul, through whom God did extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11), left a sick friend behind because he was too ill to travel. He did not heal him. Healing was never a technique the apostles could operate at will, and this small logistical note is one of the plainest proofs of it.

“Do your best to come before winter.” The Mediterranean closed to shipping from roughly November to March. If Timothy missed the season he would not arrive until spring, and Paul did not expect to be alive. Behind the practical instruction is a man counting weeks — and we do not know whether Timothy made it.

Four names follow whom we meet nowhere else: “Eubulus, Pudens, Linus and Claudia” — Roman Christians, a household perhaps, keeping company with a condemned man when Demas would not. So the letter that records the desertion of Asia and of Demas ends with a short list of people who stayed.

And then the final line, and it is the last sentence of Paul's that we possess: “The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.”

The first half is singular — to Timothy, personally, the young man who was frightened and told to fan the fire into flame. The second is plural: grace be with you all. At the very end he turns from his friend to the whole room, as he did at the close of the first letter.

The last written word of the apostle to the Gentiles is grace. After the shipwrecks and the floggings, the churches and the arguments, the deposit guarded and handed on, the desertions and the cloak left at Troas — grace. It is the only word he ever ended with, and it is the right one.
